unit.title: Develop and apply conversational skills in a foreign language

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Why is it useful for villa and hotel staff in Jamaica to learn some Spanish?
options: Spanish is an official language in Jamaica
Guests must speak Spanish to stay in a hotel
Many guests, and many resort owners, speak Spanish
Spanish is needed to read the room price list

It makes the guest feel welcome and shows them respect

essays.stem: Explain why staff who work in Jamaican villas, hotels and attractions should learn some Spanish, French or German, and how this helps both the guest and the business.
essays.modelAnswer: Jamaica welcomes visitors from many countries. Besides English speakers from North America and Britain, many guests come from Spain and Latin America, from French-speaking Canada and France, and from Germany. Many resorts in Jamaica are also owned or managed by Spanish companies, so staff may hear Spanish from managers too. When a guest is greeted in their own language, even with "Buenos días" or "Bonjour", they feel welcome, respected and more relaxed. Simple phrases help staff understand requests, give directions, take orders and spot problems quickly, so mistakes are fewer and the guest feels safe. This leads to good reviews, guests who come back and tell their friends, and better tips for staff. For the business it is a selling point that wins more visitors from those markets. For the worker, it is a skill that can lead to promotion.
markingPoints: Names Jamaica's main foreign-language visitor markets (Spanish, French, German speakers)
Guests feel welcome and respected when greeted in their own language
Fewer mistakes: requests, orders, directions and problems understood
Business benefits: good reviews, repeat guests, more visitors
Personal benefits for the worker: tips, confidence, promotion

essays.stem: Describe how you would greet a Spanish-speaking couple and begin their check-in. Give the Spanish phrases you would use and say what each one means.
essays.modelAnswer: I stand up, smile and make eye contact as they arrive. If it is morning, I say "Buenos días, señor, señora" (good morning, sir, madam); in the afternoon "Buenas tardes" and at night "Buenas noches". Then I say "Bienvenidos a Jamaica" (welcome to Jamaica) and "Me llamo Kerry-Ann" (my name is Kerry-Ann). I ask "¿Tiene una reservación?" (do you have a reservation?) and then "Su pasaporte, por favor" (your passport, please). While I check the booking, I say "Un momento, por favor" (one moment, please). When I hand back the passport I say "Gracias" (thank you). I use "usted", the polite form of "you", and not "tú". If I need to explain something I cannot say in Spanish, I ask "¿Habla inglés?" (do you speak English?) or get a colleague who speaks Spanish. At the end I say "Que disfruten su estancia" (enjoy your stay).
markingPoints: Correct greeting for the time of day (buenos días, buenas tardes, buenas noches)
Welcome and introduction (bienvenidos; me llamo)
Asks for the reservation and passport politely (por favor), with meanings
Uses usted, the polite form
Courtesy and closing (un momento, gracias, enjoy your stay) or gets help when stuck

essays.stem: A guest speaks to you in a language you know only a little. Describe what you can do so that you both understand each other.
essays.modelAnswer: First I stay calm, smile and listen carefully, and I greet the guest in their language if I can. I speak slowly and clearly, using short, simple words and no Jamaican slang. If I do not understand, I am honest: I say "Lo siento, no entiendo" and ask "¿Puede repetir, por favor?" or "Más despacio, por favor" (more slowly, please). I use gestures, such as pointing to the lift or holding up fingers for numbers. I write numbers, times and prices on paper so there is no mistake. I can use the property's phrase card, a picture menu, a map, or a translation app on my phone. If the matter is important, such as a complaint, a payment or a health problem, I ask a colleague who speaks the language or my supervisor to help. At the end I repeat what I understood, to check it is right, and I thank the guest for their patience.
markingPoints: Stays calm and polite; speaks slowly with simple words, no slang
Is honest about not understanding and asks the guest to repeat or slow down
Uses gestures, writing numbers, maps, picture menus or phrase cards
Uses a translation app, colleague or supervisor, especially for important matters
Checks understanding by repeating back; thanks the guest

essays.stem: Explain the polite and the friendly ways of saying "you" in Spanish, French and German, and say why staff should use the polite forms with guests.
essays.modelAnswer: Spanish, French and German each have two ways of saying "you". In Spanish, "tú" is the friendly form used with family, friends and children, and "usted" is the polite form used with people you do not know well or older people. In French, "tu" is friendly and "vous" is polite. In German, "du" is friendly and "Sie", written with a capital S, is polite. Staff should always use the polite form with guests: usted, vous or Sie. Using the friendly form with a stranger can sound rude or too familiar, especially to older guests and guests from Germany or France. The polite form shows respect, keeps the relationship professional and matches the titles we use, such as Señor or Señora, Monsieur or Madame, and Herr or Frau with the surname. If a guest asks you to use the friendly form, you may follow their lead.
markingPoints: Spanish: tú (friendly) and usted (polite)
French: tu (friendly) and vous (polite)
German: du (friendly) and Sie (polite)
Polite forms show respect and keep service professional
Uses titles with the surname; may follow the guest's lead if invited

essays.stem: A Spanish-speaking guest asks where the restaurant is. Describe how you would give simple directions in Spanish, with the phrases you would use.
essays.modelAnswer: I smile and say "Sí, con mucho gusto" (yes, with pleasure). I keep the directions short and simple and point the way as I speak. I use words such as "todo recto" (straight on), "a la derecha" (to the right), "a la izquierda" (to the left), "arriba" (upstairs) and "abajo" (downstairs). For example: "El restaurante está todo recto y a la izquierda, al lado de la piscina" (the restaurant is straight on and on the left, next to the pool). If it is on another floor, I say "Tome el ascensor" (take the lift) and give the floor number. I can show the place on the property map. I check the guest understood, and if the way is hard to explain, I walk with the guest to the restaurant if my duties allow. I finish with "Buen provecho" (enjoy your meal).
markingPoints: Polite opening (con mucho gusto) and a smile
Correct words for straight on, right, left, upstairs or downstairs
A simple direction sentence in Spanish, with pointing
Uses a map, or escorts the guest if needed
Checks understanding and closes politely

essays.stem: Describe how you would take a breakfast order at a villa from a Spanish-speaking guest, using simple Spanish phrases.
essays.modelAnswer: I greet the guest with "Buenos días, señora" and offer the menu. I ask "¿Qué desea para el desayuno?" (what would you like for breakfast?). I can point to items on the menu and say their names, such as "huevos" (eggs), "pan" (bread), "fruta" (fruit), and Jamaican dishes such as ackee and saltfish, which I explain simply. For drinks I ask "¿Café o té?" (coffee or tea?) and "¿Con leche? ¿Con azúcar?" (with milk? with sugar?). I also ask "¿Tiene alguna alergia?" (do you have any allergy?). I write the order down and repeat it back, pointing to the menu, so that we both agree. I say "Un momento, por favor" while I check anything I am unsure of, and "Gracias" when the order is complete. When I serve the food, I say "Buen provecho".
markingPoints: Polite greeting for the time of day and offers the menu
Asks what the guest would like, using simple phrases or pointing
Asks about drinks and extras (coffee or tea, milk, sugar)
Asks about allergies
Writes the order, repeats it back, thanks the guest and wishes them buen provecho

essays.stem: A guest who speaks only Spanish suddenly feels very ill by the pool. Explain what you would do and the Spanish words that would help.
essays.modelAnswer: The guest's safety comes first, so I must not wait because of the language. I stay with the guest and call for help at once, using the property's emergency procedure: I alert my supervisor, the first aider and, if needed, the ambulance. I speak calmly and slowly and use simple words: "¿Está bien?" (are you all right?), "¿Qué le pasa?" (what is wrong?), "¿Dónde le duele?" (where does it hurt?) and "Tranquilo" or "Tranquila" (stay calm). I tell the guest "Viene un médico" (a doctor is coming). I ask "¿Tiene alguna alergia?" and "¿Toma medicinas?" (do you take medicine?), and I look for a family member who can translate. A colleague who speaks Spanish or a translation app can help, but I never delay first aid. I keep other guests back, give the first aider the facts, and help write the incident report afterwards.
markingPoints: Safety first: does not delay help because of language
Follows the emergency procedure: stays with the guest, calls supervisor or first aider or ambulance
Uses simple Spanish to check the guest (está bien, qué le pasa, dónde le duele)
Asks about allergies or medicine, or finds family, a colleague or an app to translate
Keeps calm, hands over to the first aider and helps with the incident report

essays.stem: Describe ways a worker can keep improving their foreign-language skills at work and at home.
essays.modelAnswer: A worker can carry a small phrase book or a phrase card with the most useful words for their job, such as greetings, please and thank you, numbers and the names of items like towels and keys. They can learn a few new words every day and practise them aloud. At work, they can listen to how guests and colleagues who speak the language say things, and ask colleagues to correct them. They can practise role plays of check-in, ordering and directions with workmates. At home, they can use free language apps on a phone, watch films, news or music in Spanish, French or German with subtitles, and label things in the house with the foreign word. Joining a class, such as those offered through the Centre or tourism training, helps too. Using the language with real guests, even a little, is the best practice, because the worker learns from the guests' replies.
markingPoints: Phrase card or phrase book for the job
Regular practice of new words aloud
Learning from guests and colleagues; role plays at work
Apps, films, music or news at home
Classes or training; using the language with real guests

essays.stem: Give the greetings for morning, afternoon and evening, and the word for "goodbye", in Spanish, French and German, and explain when each is used.
essays.modelAnswer: In Spanish, "Buenos días" is used in the morning until about midday, "Buenas tardes" in the afternoon and early evening, and "Buenas noches" at night, both to greet and to say good night. "Adiós" means goodbye, and "Hasta luego" means see you later. In French, "Bonjour" is used all through the day, morning and afternoon. "Bonsoir" is used in the evening, and "Bonne nuit" only when someone is going to bed. "Au revoir" means goodbye. In German, "Guten Morgen" is used in the morning, "Guten Tag" during the day, "Guten Abend" in the evening and "Gute Nacht" at bedtime. "Auf Wiedersehen" is the polite goodbye, and "Tschüss" is friendlier. With guests I add the title, such as "Buenos días, señora", "Bonjour, Monsieur" or "Guten Morgen, Frau Weber".
markingPoints: Spanish: buenos días, buenas tardes, buenas noches, adiós
French: bonjour, bonsoir (bonne nuit at bedtime), au revoir
German: Guten Morgen, Guten Tag, Guten Abend, Auf Wiedersehen
Says correctly when each greeting is used
Adds a polite title with the greeting

essays.stem: Explain some differences in culture and custom that staff should know when serving guests from Spain, Latin America, France and Germany.
essays.modelAnswer: Many guests from these countries write the date as day, month and year, so 05/08 means 5 August, not 8 May. They often use the 24-hour clock, so 19:30 means 7:30 in the evening, and some use a comma in prices where we use a point. Staff should confirm dates, times and prices in writing to avoid mistakes. Titles matter: use Señor or Señora, Monsieur or Madame, and Herr or Frau with the surname, and the polite form of "you". Spanish and Latin American guests may greet with a kiss on the cheek among friends, but staff should keep to a smile or handshake and follow the property's rules. Many German guests value being on time, so tours and transfers should leave when promised. Dinner may be eaten later by Spanish guests. Staff should never make jokes about a guest's country or copy their accent, and should avoid slang the guest will not understand.
markingPoints: Date order (day, month, year) and the 24-hour clock
Confirms dates, times and prices in writing
Uses titles and the polite form of address
Knows customs such as greetings, punctuality and meal times, keeping professional
Avoids slang, jokes or stereotypes about a guest's country

practical1.title: Role play: welcome and check-in in Spanish, with a phrase card
practical1.brief: Your group will first make a Spanish phrase card (on card or a poster, or on a phone or computer) for welcoming guests and checking them in at a villa or hotel. It must show at least 15 phrases, each with the Spanish (with its accents and question marks) and the English meaning, grouped as: greetings and welcome; courtesy (please, thank you, sorry, one moment); check-in questions; and directions. Then act out the arrival and check-in of a Spanish-speaking couple in four stages: greeting and welcome at the door; check-in at the desk (reservation, passport, form); giving directions to the room, pool and restaurant; and saying goodbye. Take turns: every member plays the staff member in at least one stage while the others play the guests or take notes, and every member speaks Spanish in the role play. The assessor may play a guest and ask one unexpected question. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and the notes to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Card or poster paper and markers, or a computer or phone to make the phrase card
A Spanish-English phrase book or dictionary (an app may be used to check spelling)
A made-up booking, a blank registration form and a made-up passport card (no real documents)
A desk, two chairs and a property map
Note paper and pens for the observers
photos: The finished phrase card, close enough to read
Stage 1: greeting and welcome at the door
Stage 2: check-in at the desk, with the form
Stage 3: giving directions with the map
The observers' notes after the role play
checklist: Helped make the phrase card, with correct Spanish spelling and accents
Used the correct greeting for the time of day
Used the polite form (usted) and a title (señor or señora)
Said please, thank you and one moment in Spanish at the right times
Asked at least one check-in question in Spanish clearly and slowly
Gave or understood a simple direction (right, left, straight on)
Handled a phrase they did not understand politely (asked to repeat or got help)
Kept a friendly, professional manner: smile, eye contact, open posture
safety: Use only made-up names, bookings and documents; never real guest or trainee ID details
Keep the role-play area clear of bags and cables so no one trips
If you use a phone or computer, keep cables tidy and follow the Centre's rules for devices
Speak to each other with respect: no jokes about any country, accent or person

practical2.title: Courtesy poster and dinner-service role play in Spanish, French and German
practical2.brief: Your group will make a courtesy poster for a villa staff room that shows, in Spanish, French and German, how to say: good morning, good evening, welcome, please, thank you, you're welcome, excuse me, sorry, enjoy your meal and goodbye, with the English beside each and the accents spelt correctly. Then act out a dinner service on the villa verandah for three guests: one speaks Spanish, one French and one German. Every member serves at least one guest: greet them in their language, seat them, take a simple drinks order, serve, handle one request (for example more water, or the bill) and say goodbye. Members who are not serving play the guests or take notes. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and the notes to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Poster paper and markers, or a computer and printer
Phrase books or dictionaries for Spanish, French and German
A table laid for three, menus, a jug of water, glasses and a tray
An order pad and pens; note paper for the observers
photos: The finished courtesy poster, close enough to read
Guests greeted and seated in their own languages
A drinks order being taken and written down
Goodbye at the end of the service, and the observers' notes
checklist: Helped make the poster, with correct spelling and accents in all three languages
Greeted their guest in the guest's own language, with a title
Used the polite form of "you" (usted, vous or Sie)
Took and repeated back a simple order using phrases or pointing
Said please, thank you and enjoy your meal in the guest's language
Handled the guest's request correctly, or got help politely
Said goodbye correctly in the guest's language
Kept a friendly, professional manner throughout
safety: Carry the tray safely, with heavy items in the centre, and keep the floor dry
Use plastic or unbreakable glasses for the role play if the Centre prefers
Keep walkways clear of bags and chairs
Speak with respect: no jokes about any country, accent or person
